title: The Girl and the Sea Beneath the Cliff
summary: At Lyme Regis, on England's southern coast, the sea worked on the cliffs every day.

chapters.title: The Girl and the Sea Beneath the Cliff

paragraphs.text: At Lyme Regis, on England's southern coast, the sea worked on the cliffs every day.
Waves struck their base. Rain loosened the layers above. After storms, pieces of rock lay on the beach where there had been clear ground before.
Inside those rocks were remains of another sea, one that had covered the area roughly two hundred million years earlier.
Mary Anning grew up beside the cliffs.
Her family had little money. Her father, Richard, was a carpenter who also collected fossils to sell. Visitors bought curled ammonites and pointed belemnites as curiosities.
Mary and her brother Joseph learned to search the beach. A piece of fossil exposed in a rock could mean something worth selling, and selling it could help pay for food.
But finding a fossil was only the beginning.
The object had to be removed without breaking it. A hammer used carelessly could destroy the evidence. A valuable skeleton might remain hidden beneath heavy rock, with only a small part showing.
The cliffs themselves were dangerous. The same falls that exposed fossils could bury a collector beneath them.
Richard died in 1810, leaving the family in difficult circumstances.
Early in the following years, Joseph found an unusual fossil skull. Mary went on to uncover the associated skeleton, a job that required prolonged work rather than one dramatic swing of a hammer.
The creature was about five metres long.
Its long jaws and large eye sockets were unlike the familiar shells sold to visitors. Scientists examined the remains and argued about the animal to which they had belonged.
It became an important early specimen in the scientific study of ichthyosaurs.
An ichthyosaur was a marine reptile. It was not a dinosaur, and it was not a fish, even though its body was adapted for moving through water.
The distinction mattered. Scientists were beginning to reconstruct groups of animals that no longer existed.
Some people still explained unfamiliar fossils as the remains of creatures living in undiscovered places. Increasing evidence showed that many fossil animals had vanished altogether.
Extinction meant Earth's living world had changed profoundly.

Mary continued collecting. She learned anatomy, compared bones, read scientific writing, and prepared specimens with care. Her work increasingly required recognising what a fragment belonged to and where other parts might be found.
In 1823, she uncovered another remarkable skeleton.
It had four flippers, a small head, and a very long neck.
This was a plesiosaur.
The arrangement looked so unfamiliar that Georges Cuvier, one of Europe's leading experts on fossil animals, initially questioned whether it was genuine.
A long neck attached to that body could seem like a mistake made by combining remains from different animals.
The position of the bones was therefore important. An articulated skeleton, with its parts preserved in their natural arrangement, provided much stronger evidence than a box of loose pieces.
Further examination convinced Cuvier that the specimen was real.
Mary's discovery supplied a body plan scientists could study. Plesiosaurs were no longer merely an incomplete collection of difficult bones.
Fossils also carried information about the environment in which they had lived.
The rock layers at Lyme Regis contained ammonites, marine reptiles, and other sea creatures. Those remains showed that a beach below cliffs had once been part of a seabed.
Sediment had covered dead organisms. Over immense spans of time, buried material and minerals preserved traces of their bodies while the surrounding sediment became rock.
Later movements of Earth's crust and erosion brought those layers to the surface.
Mary did not know every modern detail of these processes. But the evidence she uncovered helped make the ancient environment visible.
In 1828, she found remains of a flying reptile, a pterosaur, the first such discovery outside Germany.
Her finds were no longer only about animals swimming in a lost sea. They also revealed creatures that had flown above it.

Other observations opened smaller windows into ancient life. Fossilised dung, called coprolites, could preserve pieces of food. What seemed an unappealing object could help identify what an animal had eaten.
The scientific importance of Mary's work did not remove the social barriers around her.
She was a woman from a poor family, earning money by selling specimens. Scientific societies and formal education offered far more opportunities to wealthy men.
The Geological Society of London did not admit women as fellows during her lifetime. Researchers who bought her fossils sometimes published descriptions without giving her appropriate credit.
Yet collecting and preparing were central parts of the discovery. A skeleton destroyed during extraction would never reach a scientist's desk.

Henry De la Beche, a geologist who knew Mary, painted a reconstruction of the ancient Dorset sea in 1830. His picture included marine reptiles based on fossil evidence. Prints were sold to help support her.
The image allowed people to connect separate skeletons with a shared environment.
Mary died in 1847, aged forty-seven. She had not become wealthy, despite her extraordinary contributions.
Her specimens remained.

They were studied again as scientific knowledge grew. Some can still be seen in museum galleries, where their flippers, jaws, and long necks continue to explain a world far older than the buildings containing them.
The cliffs at Lyme Regis are still eroding.

The sea continues uncovering the seabed of another age. Mary Anning helped turn what emerged from that rock into evidence of real animals, real environments, and changes stretching across millions of years.
